meta.title: Who really said "I Take My Only Exercise Acting as a Pallbearer to My Friends Who Exercise"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain, and almost certainly not Chauncey Depew. The joke was in newspapers by 1925, and the earliest evidence points to editor William Allen White.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Take My Only Exercise Acting as a Pallbearer to My Friends Who Exercise'?
meta.ogDescription: Depew died in 1928; the credit to him starts in 1930. Quote Investigator's earliest instance is William Allen White in January 1925.

answer.label: Not Chauncey Depew — most likely William Allen White
answer.authorDates: 1868–1944 · American newspaper editor, author and Progressive-movement leader
answer.sourceLine: Chauncey Depew died on 5 April 1928, and Quote Investigator ↗ finds the joke credited to him only from 1930 onward. Its earliest instance of the gag is the Kansas newspaperman William Allen White, in the Evening Republican of 14 January 1925: he got his exercise “by acting as pallbearer for golfers who exercise to prolong useless lives.” QI calls White the leading candidate — and says plainly that any ascription would be tentative.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the Depew credit is posthumous, and even the leading alternative is offered tentatively.

source.excerpt: I get my exercise by acting as pallbearer for golfers who exercise to prolong useless lives.
trail: Quote Investigator’s survey of the joke ↗ lays out the chronology. It opens with a looser precursor — Ring Lardner, in Cosmopolitan in August 1922, on locals who “get plenty of exercise dodging Flivingos and acting as pall bearers” — then the joke proper: William Allen White in the Evening Republican on 14 January 1925, and Royal S. Copeland in the Chester Times on 26 June 1926. Its conclusion: “the earliest evidence currently points to William Allen White as originator because he expressed the core of the joke by 1925.”

The same page dates the two famous credits: “By 1930 the humorous remark was credited to Chauncey Depew, and by 1950 the jest was assigned to Mark Twain.” QI is blunt about both — “Depew was credited with the jest after he had been dead two years” and “the first citation for Mark Twain occurred in 1950, forty years after his death.” Wikipedia gives Depew’s dates as 23 April 1834 – 5 April 1928 ↗ and Wikiquote gives Twain’s as 1835–1910 ↗, which is exactly what those two intervals come to.

We read Wikiquote’s Chauncey Depew page ↗ in full. It does list “I get my exercise acting as pallbearer to my friends who exercise” — but its only citation is a 1958 collection, Four Talks for Bibliophiles, page 70, thirty years after Depew died. It offers no contemporary source, and the page carries no Misattributed or Disputed section at all.
We also checked Wikiquote’s Mark Twain page ↗, which maintains large sourced, disputed and misattributed sections: the pallbearer joke appears in none of them.
source.excerptNote: That is the 1925 wording Quote Investigator gives for William Allen White in the Evening Republican — the earliest instance of the joke it documents. The smoother line people repeat today is closer to Senator Royal S. Copeland’s 1926 version in the Chester Times: “The only exercise I take is acting as pall-bearer to my friends who have indulged in strenuous exercise!” We could not reach scans of either newspaper ourselves; both wordings and both locators come from QI’s chronology ↗

source.rightsNote: Every documented appearance of the joke that this page relies on — Ring Lardner in 1922, William Allen White in January 1925, Royal S. Copeland in June 1926 — was published in a United States newspaper or magazine well before 1931, so those wordings are in the public domain and may be quoted freely. The smoothed modern retelling has no single fixed source of its own.

author.name: William Allen White
author.heading: About William Allen White
author.metaLine: 1868–1944 · American newspaper editor, author and leader of the Progressive movement
author.bio: William Allen White (1868–1944) was an American newspaper editor, politician and author, and a leader of the Progressive movement; from 1896 until his death he was read as a spokesman for middle America. He was a fixture of the Kansas press — at a 1937 banquet in his honour the Kansas Editorial Association called him “the most loved and most distinguished member” of it. The pallbearer joke is not one of the things he is remembered for, and he did not firmly claim it — Quote Investigator notes that “White himself expressed uncertainty in his 1940 letter.” His 1925 line is simply the earliest instance anyone has yet documented.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two famous names collected this joke after their deaths, and a third used it in life without ever claiming it.

items.why: Depew — senator, railroad president and celebrated after-dinner speaker — died on 5 April 1928. Quote Investigator ↗ records that “by 1930 the humorous remark was credited to Chauncey Depew,” and traces the joke itself back to 1925, in another man’s mouth. Even Wikiquote ↗ can cite the line to him only through a 1958 book.

Twain is the default owner of any orphaned American wisecrack. QI dates the Twain ascription to 1950 ↗, and Wikiquote’s Twain page ↗ — which tracks his disputed and misattributed lines carefully — does not carry it in any section.

Copeland, a physician and United States senator, gave the joke its smoothest early form in the Chester Times on 26 June 1926. But QI notes he did not claim authorship ↗, and White’s 1925 version came first.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: William Allen White, in the Evening Republican, 14 January 1925 — the earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ documents, though it calls the ascription tentative and White himself was uncertain.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The 1920s were the first decade when ordinary Americans were told, in newspapers and advertisements, that they ought to be exercising — and the joke is the backlash, arriving almost immediately. Its target in the earliest versions is specifically the golfer, the new suburban enthusiast whose devotion to his own health struck older men as faintly ridiculous.

It travelled the way newspaper jokes did: a wisecrack printed once under a real name, reprinted without one, and then reassigned to whichever famous wit the reprinting editor thought of first. That is how a Kansas editor’s gag about golfers ends up in circulation as Mark Twain’s.
context.pull: By 1930 it was Depew’s. By 1950 it was Twain’s. Both of them were dead.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's conclusion: 'the earliest evidence currently points to William Allen White as originator because he expressed the core of the joke by 1925', and any ascription would be tentative.

QI: 'By 1930 the humorous remark was credited to Chauncey Depew, and by 1950 the jest was assigned to Mark Twain.' Its conclusion adds: 'Depew was credited with the jest after he had been dead two years' and 'The first citation for Mark Twain occurred in 1950, forty years after his death' and 'White himself expressed uncertainty in his 1940 letter.'
QI's chronology opens with a looser 1922 precursor from Ring Lardner in Cosmopolitan (August 1922): locals who 'get plenty of exercise dodging Flivingos and acting as pall bearers'.

QI gives White's 1925 wording ('I get my exercise by acting as pallbearer for golfers who exercise to prolong useless lives', Evening Republican, 14 January 1925) and Copeland's 1926 wording (Chester Times, 26 June 1926).

Wikiquote's Chauncey Depew page lists 'I get my exercise acting as pallbearer to my friends who exercise', cited only to Four Talks for Bibliophiles (1958), p. 70; the page has no Misattributed or Disputed section.
Wikiquote's Mark Twain page (sourced, disputed and misattributed sections) contains no instance of the pallbearer joke.
Chauncey Mitchell Depew lived 23 April 1834 to 5 April 1928.

William Allen White lived 10 February 1868 to 29 January 1944 and was an American newspaper editor, politician, author and leader of the Progressive movement, called by the Kansas Editorial Association in 1937 'the most loved and most distinguished member' of the Kansas press.
Royal Samuel Copeland (7 November 1868 - 17 June 1938) was a physician and United States senator from New York.
